client: I've been having trouble sleeping because I can't stop thinking about my exams next week. My parents have always expected me to get top grades, and I'm terrified of disappointing them if I don't do well. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the pressure isn't going away no matter what I do.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming this feels for you, caught between your own worries and your parents' expectations. It makes sense that these thoughts would keep you up at night when they feel so important. What would it be like to imagine telling your parents about these fears?

client: The thought of telling my parents about my fears makes my stomach twist. I know they just want what's best for me, but I'm scared they'll see it as weakness or think I'm not trying hard enough. Part of me worries they'll just tell me to push through it, which would make me feel even more alone.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this burden alone because you anticipate they might not understand your struggle in the way you need them to. That fear of being dismissed or seen as inadequate must make this situation feel even heavier. What do you imagine might happen if they responded with compassion instead of pressure?

client:
I don't know if I can even imagine them responding with compassion anymore. Every time I've tried opening up before, they either give me empty platitudes or tell me to just "get over it." It feels safer to keep it to myself, even though that makes me feel so alone. 

Part of me wants to believe they could understand, but the evidence says otherwise. Why set myself up for more disappointment?
therapist: It's understandable you'd protect yourself by keeping these feelings inside when past attempts to share them haven't felt truly heard. That pattern of dismissal must make it incredibly hard to hold onto hope for a different response. What would it feel like to acknowledge that their limitations might say more about them than about your worthiness of support?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard not to take it personally when people keep dismissing me. Even if it's their limitation, it still leaves me feeling alone and like my feelings don't matter. Part of me wants to believe I deserve support, but the evidence keeps pointing the other way. 

I guess I'm just tired of having to be the one who understands everyone else's limitations while my needs keep getting pushed aside. It feels like another way of telling me to just deal with it on my own.
therapist: You're naming such an important pain point—the exhausting reality of constantly making space for others' limitations while your own needs go unmet. That imbalance would naturally leave anyone feeling depleted and questioning their worth. What might it look like to start redirecting some of that understanding you give others back toward yourself?

client: I don't know... it just feels selfish to focus on myself like that. Whenever I try to put my needs first, I immediately feel guilty, like I'm letting people down or being a bad friend. The thought of redirecting that energy toward myself makes me anxious—what if people think I'm being self-centered?
therapist: It sounds like you've internalized this belief that self-care equals selfishness, which must make it incredibly hard to prioritize your own wellbeing. That automatic guilt shows how deeply you've learned to put others first—what might it be like to challenge that assumption that meeting your needs means failing others?

client:
I know logically that self-care isn't selfish, but I still feel guilty when I take time for myself. Like if I say no to helping a friend because I'm exhausted, I spend the whole time thinking about how I let them down. It's like my brain won't accept that I deserve care too. 

The idea of challenging that belief makes me anxious—what if I start prioritizing myself and people think I'm being self-centered? I've always been the reliable one who puts others first.
therapist: It's powerful that you can recognize this gap between what you know logically and what you feel emotionally—that shows real self-awareness. The fear of being seen differently if you start setting boundaries must make this change feel risky when your identity has been tied to being the reliable one. What would it be like to start with one small act of self-care and observe what actually happens, rather than what you fear might happen?

client: I get what you're saying about starting small, but even that feels scary. What if my family thinks I'm being selfish or stops relying on me? That's always been my role - the one who keeps everything together. The idea of putting myself first even in small ways makes me feel guilty, like I'm letting everyone down.
therapist: It sounds like your role as the family stabilizer has become such a core part of your identity that any change feels threatening, even when you know you're running on empty. That guilt you describe—how might it help to explore where those "shoulds" about always being the strong one originally came from?

client:
I never really thought about where those "shoulds" came from... I guess it started when my parents divorced and I had to take care of my younger siblings. But even knowing that doesn't make the guilt go away - it feels like if I stop being the strong one now, everything will fall apart. 

Part of me wants to explore this, but another part is scared that if I look too closely at these feelings, I'll realize I've been doing everything wrong all these years.
therapist: It's understandable to feel that fear—like examining these patterns might somehow undo all the strength and care you've shown over the years. What if instead of "doing everything wrong," this exploration could be about honoring how much you've carried while also making space for your own needs? What might it feel like to approach this with curiosity rather than judgment?

client: I get what you're saying about approaching this with curiosity, but it's hard not to judge myself. When I think about all the years I've put others first, part of me feels angry that I let myself get to this point. The idea of making space for my needs almost feels selfish after so long.
therapist: It sounds like there's a mix of anger and regret surfacing as you reflect on how much you've put others' needs before your own—that's such a natural reaction when we start to recognize patterns of self-neglect. What might it be like to hold that anger gently, as a sign that part of you is finally ready to advocate for what you deserve?

client: I get what you're saying about the anger being a sign, but honestly it just makes me feel more guilty. Like now I'm angry at people I care about, and that feels wrong. It's like no matter what I do—putting others first or feeling angry about it—I end up feeling bad.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful options—suppressing your needs and feeling drained, or acknowledging them and feeling guilty. That's such a difficult place to be. What if this guilt isn't a sign you're doing something wrong, but rather evidence of how deeply you've learned to prioritize others' comfort over your own?
